en: {The Rite of Initiation for Amṛteśvara, extracted from an ancient palm-leaf manuscript} In the Mata taught by Netrāmṛtabhairava, the Great Kaulakeya, he stands pervading [the world] and [protecting it] from evil deeds. 5.

But He, who is the conqueror of death, eternally delights in bestowing the fruits of enjoyment upon the universe while remaining within the state of being veiled through His manifestation as the ten-fold form and His sovereign power;
thus, by sprinkling the nectar-water of compassion, He awakens those caught in the cycle of worldly existence.
May the Lord Amṛteśa protect us, appearing in the form of the elephant of the venerable Guru. || 6 ||
I bow to Mahādeva, who is the form of light, auspicious, peaceful, the supreme nectar, the Lord of immortality, and endowed with glory. 7.
Bearing on his left lap the Great Goddess Śrī, the sole mother of the world,
he was made to tremble by the wonder of supreme bliss.
I constantly pay homage with devotion through speech, action,
and mind to the Lord of Supreme Nectar, the pure light, blissful, stainless, and all-pervading.

Having thoroughly understood the excellent Āgama of Maheśvara as it was spoken by the preeminent gurus in due order, I shall compose this commentary on the worship of Amṛtabhairava for the sake of those who suffer.
I, Viśveśvara, shall now describe according to the prescribed rite the initiation (dīkṣā) for Bhairava, whose name begins with "Mṛtyuñjaya," who is the essence of nectar.
Having first learned from the mouth of the Guru, then from the divine Śāmbhava Āgama,
and subsequently from one's own experience, [the dissolution of the mantra] was taught by Vighneśvara;
now the procedure for initiation into the Lord Amṛtabhairava is written down according to the rule.
Through the purification of the reality of the objects and so forth, liberation is attained for the disciple from another [the teacher]. || 12 ||
Thus ends the salutation.

Longevity, the state of being a medicinal herb, birth in auspicious regions with a wealthy body, motherly affection for one’s offspring even in gambling, and the absence of desire for the path due to great gain—he who possessed these has died. (1)
Having attained a human birth in this cycle of existence, one finds excellence of birth in a good land;
even there, one possesses unimpaired limbs and a desire for dharma that is free from worldly longing.
For one whose devotion toward the Guru, the Deity, the Liṅgin, the Preceptor, and likewise the Sādhaka, remains unsurpassed, that is the true fruit of birth.
Having attained human birth— a status difficult even for the gods to obtain—
those men who worship Bhairava, known as Amṛteśa, become immortal.
When one sets out with the desire to accomplish that which results in success,
one should then worship the Lord Śiva, the Sovereign of Immortality, with devotion.
Thus ends the praise of human birth.

In this cycle of existence, which is as terrifying as a mass of water bubbles and is most exceedingly dreadful, those of dull intellect, being attached to sense objects, fall again and again due to delusion. (1)

In this perishable world, those attached to sense objects constantly nourish the thought "I am" through such contemplation; out of delusion, they maintain their bodies until the final collapse, which is like honey mixed with poison.
Having entered this most unstable, terrible, and fearsome cycle of existence (saṃsāra),
those men who do not worship Śiva become inhabitants of hell.
Thus ends the censure of saṃsāra.
The pitiless Yama leads away the wealthy, the proud, the heroic, the handsome, the sweet-spoken, the young, the adolescent, and the old alike. (1)
A man who is proficient in Vedic knowledge yet remains a fool, even if he is a composer of poetry.
And Yama, mercilessly leads away even the sovereign emperor of the whole earth.
Having cast the snare-net around his neck, Death, greatly delighted, kills him with a mallet and leads the son of Manu away in an instant. || 3 ||
"House, wealth, sons, wife, kinsmen, pleasures, and kingdoms— all these born of karma—
human beings must abandon everything and depart at their own death, accompanied by their auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
Thus ends the section on impermanence.

The Illusionist (Māyī), having completely cast aside the animal fetter and the karmic fetter, and because he delivers [beings] from the mouth of death by means of the protection provided by the restraining net,
is therefore proclaimed as Mṛtyujit (the Conqueror of Death); and he is endowed with the splendor of Lakṣmī.
He is remembered as Amṛtīśa because he bestows upon his devotees the state of immortality and the path to yoga. || 1 ||
Therefore, the goddess Śrī, having taken [him] by the hand according to the prescribed rite,
bestowed the initiation that grants the enjoyment of liberation and bestows the state beyond mind (unmana).

As long as the self is not stainless, it is said to be within the Śaiva [system]; however, when situated upon the petals, the person knows everything, transcending all that is free from disease. || 3 ||
I shall restrain the collection of my senses; O Goddess, that reality characterized by power will not become stainless as long as it has not been purified.
Those who, by means of the fire of initiation and knowledge, purify themselves until they are stainless, know nothing other than the supreme state. || 5 ||
The rudrākṣa rosary, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), worship, and the recitation of mantras;
the offering of oblations, flowers, fire-sacrifice (homa), and likewise meditation. || 6 ||
For one who lacks initiation (dīkṣā), consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and ritual bathing (snapana) are indeed fruitless;
what then is the use of other multitudes of mantras or the propitiation of deities? (7)
Wherever the Lord of the gods is meditated upon, recited, and worshipped with devotion once initiation has been performed, there He is present.
Thousands of killings of Brahmins, hundreds of killings of cows, women, and children,
and all other sins are destroyed once the initiation for liberation has been performed.
Thus, the greatness of initiation consists in its being the means for purifying one's own power.
Now he states the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple.
Born in an auspicious place, possessing an auspicious foundation, virtuous in speech and conduct, he is the auspicious awakener of the path. (1)
He who produces delight at the mere sight of him, who is endowed with all limbs, who has practiced all the scriptures, and who sets forth all paths. || 2 ||

He understands the distinction between the *kula* and *akula*, possesses his own spiritual lineage, and is endowed with prosperity; ever rejoicing in the bliss of the Command (*ājñā*), he has reached the further shore of the vision of Śiva. (3)
Free from greed for wealth and other such things, he is a renunciant who provides refuge to all people;
though established in a state beyond conventional conduct, he is a protector of true compassion.

The Guru who has arrived through the sequence of the Krama path and is proficient in the flood of higher consciousness is Śiva himself, the direct liberator from the bonds of worldly existence. || 5 ||
Even by a disciple of little merit and dull intellect,
he should be served with his threefold self— through action, mind, and speech.

Thinking "He is Śiva," one who is bound by the fetters [of worldly existence] should prostrate with falls of the staff (daṇḍapāta), endowed with a mind full of devotion, having first prepared a mandala before him.
Whatever is most dear to him, and by whatever means he finds satisfaction—that the disciple should take refuge in, because of his habit of propitiating that very thing. (8)
Having entered and carefully observed the inner disposition of the heart,
one should perform every task desired by the guru in a manner that is not ostentatious.
One should offer everything— wealth, wife, body, and so forth—
and clearly propitiate the guru with the single-minded disposition of sharing both happiness and suffering.
When a disciple is engaged in the propitiation of the Guru, those who have attained perfection in the past become filled with compassion and eager to bestow spiritual accomplishments.
Therefore, having cast aside all pretense, one should in every way cultivate internal meditation;
one who has no other refuge should go for shelter to Śambhu, whose very form is the Guru. 12.
For here, indeed, blinded people who are deluded suffer;
even though a guru is present, they serve the king out of a desire for wealth. (13)
Even while undergoing hardships and even by sacrificing their very lives,
they do not obtain any fruit whatsoever, either in this world or in the next.
How could one whose intellect is exceedingly pure and who abides in discernment abandon the Guru, the very embodiment of Śiva, to serve a king? (15)
There is a great difference between the universal monarch and the preceptor:
one is the lord of a single province, while the other is the sovereign of all principles. (16)
A king, when pleased, gives a mere village with great difficulty;
but the Guru, from the fire up to the limit of Śiva, gives everything with ease. (17)
Just as the two fruits of a tree are not difficult to obtain when its root is watered, even so, when a guru is propitiated, the perfections already established [in the past] flourish. (18)
He who strives for the state of liberation without serving his guru is like one who desires fruits from trees that have not yet been planted. (19)
Why do Brahmā and the other foremost gods, the Rudras, Śambhu, and the lords of the forest, bestow their grace [only] when the Guru has not yet been served? (20)
When the Guru has been properly propitiated with joy, tranquility, and compassion,
all the deities become eager to bestow their grace upon the practitioner.
Therefore, by one who has no other refuge and who desires the path to perfection, Śiva—who has manifested in person—should always be served within the form of the Guru. 22.
Even by the gurus, an examination of the disciple must first be made clearly;
for the fitness of unexamined disciples is not established in the perfected teaching.
Sometimes it was excellent, sometimes it was of this kind;
sometimes the speech was pleasant, and sometimes it consisted of harsh syllables. (24)
Sometimes he should be brought inside; sometimes he should be sent outside.
Sometimes he should be highly honored; and sometimes he should even be struck. || 25 ||
Even when treated in this way, he who has a mind permeated by devotion does not fall under the sway of joy or sorrow; such a person is fit for the teachings of the Siddhas.
He who would lead his enjoyment from one day to the next,
thinking "I have achieved my goal," is worthy of the teaching of the Siddhas.
He who, even when reviled many times or even beaten,
does not abandon devotion to his guru, is worthy of the teachings of the Siddhas.
Furthermore, he who does not abandon a task for his guru—whether it be unspoken or already spoken—and who conducts himself with undivided devotion, is fit for the teaching of the Siddhas. (29)
Having examined the child hundreds of times through such modes of conduct as these, when he proves worthy through thorough examination, only then may he be accepted. (30)
One should contemplate there for eight, three, or five years;
one must not perform initiation during that time—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Of a tested disciple who is free from blemish, whose senses are subdued, who is indifferent toward wealth, women, and the body, and who has turned away from worldly existence; (32)
This knowledge should be given to one who is devoted to all beings, to a devotee of the Linga, and to one who possesses the Linga; otherwise, one would go to hell. (33)
It should not be given to those of evil character, nor to the wrathful, nor likewise to sinners, nor to those intent on reviling their gurus, nor to those who disparage the mantras of the gods. (34)
This should be given to one's own disciples and virtuous sons, but not otherwise—to atheists, to the deceitful, or to those excluded from the dharma of ritual action. (35)

One should not grant [the mantra] even to one's own beloved, unless they have received the initiation of the rules (samayadīkṣā), provided they are initiated devotees who worship the Guru, the Deity, and the Fire.
"In every way, it must not be given at all—this is the supreme command of the Lord.
O Goddess of gods, by violating this command, the fall of the body will occur. (37)
If one gives out of delusion, affection, or a desire for wealth, one goes to a terrible hell; such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
By observing the command of the Supreme Lord, one shall attain perfection;
and by such observance, O Goddess, the Supreme Lord becomes the conqueror of death. (39)
One should perform the preliminary service to the Guru for twelve years with a concentrated mind;
or having prepared the mandala, one may do so for seven, five, three, or even one year.
Either according to the sequence of the Samas, or by means of one's own devotion and through the efficacy of cause and effect,
one should construct a mandala with the nine jewels that fulfills all desires.
Alternatively, having offered with great devotion a circular seat made of gold or silver, or prepared with the four ingredients, together with a pair of golden sandals; || 42 ||
Having performed seven, five, or even three prostrations preceded by the staff-like salutation (daṇḍapraṇāma),
he should lie down upon the ground with his knees raised, remaining composed in mind.
Having filled his joined palms with white, fragrant flowers,
he then recognizes with devotion the Guru who bestows liberation.
And [grant] me, O true Guru, initiation in every way—me who am wretched and afflicted—in the auspicious family known as Nirvāṇa, which is the supreme reality. (45)
O Lord, by Your own will, grant me the initiation that bestows liberation;
once it is performed, the ocean of existence is crossed and one is truly released from bondage.
Thus, the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple, ending with the construction of the maṇḍala, have been explained.
First, the illustrious and venerable Deśika, having bathed according to the prescribed sequence and having performed the Sandhyā rites in due order with royal honors, [proceeded].

While remembering his own body as impermanent, one should adorn oneself with well-washed garments, fragrant unguents, sandalwood paste, jasmine and other flowers, incense, and auspicious powders, according to the sequence of worship that removes suffering. (2)
It was made of gold and silver, exceedingly bright and vast, beautified by hanging strings of pearls and golden garlands;
it was a place of perpetual festival, highly honored by Hari and Viriñci.
The sacrificial hall of Śambhu, who removes the fear and suffering of worldly existence. || 3 ||
The most excellent of teachers should enter the auspicious and beautiful sacrificial hall, which possesses great splendor, has four gates, and is enriched with various diverse flowers.
It was frequented by various and diverse birds and by intoxicated cuckoos;
it was covered with bowers of creepers and inhabited by yakṣas and kinnaras.
With *campaka*, *aśoka*, and *punnāga* trees, with coconut palms and *kapittha* trees, with jackfruit, mangoes, pomegranates, and *bījapūraka* fruits;
with *mātuluṅga*, *ghoṇṭā*, and *tāla* trees, and in some places with small date-palm trees.
With oranges, tamarinds, plantains, and karmaraṅkas; || 7 ||
And with *lavalī* and *karamarda* trees, as well as *jambū* and *pūga* trees,
with *tamāla*, *bilva*, and *jambīra* trees, and likewise with small *vadara* trees.
In some places it was filled with *kuravaka* trees, with clusters of *kāñjikāra* and *kadaṃbaka*,
as well as with *vakula*, *kiṃkirāta*, *pāṭala*, and *madhūka* trees.
It was adorned on all sides by multitudes of *pārijāta* trees,
as well as by *tagara*, *karavīra*, *mālatī*, *kunda*, and *yūthī* flowers.
In some places with jasmine, campaka, and other flowers, and in others with the *navamālikā*;
in some places with white water-lilies, lotuses, and *kahlāra* lilies, and in others with blue lotuses and the like.
It was adorned with holy flowers and fruits of every season,
and frequented by the lords of the gods, gandharvas, and yakṣas, as well as by vidyādharas and great serpents.
The sacrificial pavilion was attended with great diligence on all sides by the lords of the Rākṣasas, the Dānavas, the Kinnaras, and the Garuḍas.
It was attended by Apsaras and goddesses, by Kinnarīs with their songs,
and by Yakṣīs and Vidyādharīs, as well as by the sons of sages.

Immersed in the essence of the bliss of Śiva, they remained outside the sacrificial ground, praising him with devotion, palms joined in *añjali*, through songs, dances, laughter, and other such expressions.
Hāhā, Hūhū, Kumbhura, Nārada, Viśvāvasu, Citraratha, and Sumālī—by their excellent songs, they were indeed intoxicated by the essence of service to Śambhu’s sacrifice. || 16 ||
And there were those with the forms of goats, cats, elephants, owls, vultures, camels, jackals, and mice;
lords of the Gaṇas who bore the shapes of fish, lions, boars, hares, and peacocks. || 17 ||

With infinite mouths, feet, arms, and heads, and supported by those who bear a single head, it is being diligently carried away, while being fiercely protected by the hosts of the leaders of the Gaṇas. || 18 ||
By the command of Śiva, those stationed in hundreds of crores were sent by Maheśvara for long-term protection;
and the hosts of chief Gaṇas, stationed in fourteen crores, were dispatched to drive away the obstacles.
Then, at the western gate, Lakṣmī should be meditated upon as having a beautiful form,
raining down a flood of the nine jewels upon the sacrificial pavilion.
The king of weapons was blazing brightly upon the threshold, with tawny matted hair, adorned with knitted eyebrows,
and a face made terrible by its fangs.
Threatening the host of obstacles, he should then meditate upon his gurus;
having worshipped them with diligence, he may thereafter step across his own threshold.
Having entered the interior, taking hold of the left door-jamb,
he should [ward off] the flood of obstacles emerging from the center of the sacrificial hall.
Having thus reflected according to the prescribed rule, he performed the unsurpassed Śiva-sacrifice,
which consists of the great multitude of principles (tattvas) extending from Sadāśiva downwards.
What is the use of saying more here? One should meditate upon the unsurpassed, luminous pavilion of Śiva, made of gold and inlaid with jewels.
Perceiving himself as the essence of supreme bliss, with his body formed by the placement of mantras,
he should sprinkle that excellent pavilion with the water of the general *argha* offering.
One should go to the northeastern direction for the preparation of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
or else, being well-restrained, one should sit facing east or north.
One should have a very beautiful mandala made there, measuring one cubit;
upon that mandala, five beautiful bowls (sarāva) should be placed.
One should deposit the purified *kalās*, beginning with Nivṛtti, as they have been heard [in the scriptures] within that;
likewise, one should offer the seat (*āsana*) with the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Nivṛtti and the others. (29)
Cow’s urine, cow dung, clarified butter, curd, and milk, in this order,
[should be placed] in the west, north, south, east, and in the center, respectively.

With water from *kuśa* grass mixed with jewels, reciting the *Gāyatrī* which is the form of nectar, he should pour it while brandishing his rosary and thinking, "I am Śaśadhara. He should also call to mind the obstacles situated within the earth and in the intermediate space, as well as those that move through the sky. || 14 ||
One should prepare *kuśa* grass for the *vardhanī* vessel and provide a seat;
one should worship the deities named after the site (*vāstu*) in the southwest and Lakṣmī at the door.
Filling the sacrificial pavilion on all sides with jewels,
she [worshipped] Śiva, the Lord of Nectar (Amṛtīśvara), together with his limbs (attendants), in the sacrificial pit facing the west.
One should worship the God and the Goddess— who resides in the Ocean of Milk, who is seated upon a vardhanī, and who moves with the gait of a lion— and who possesses the form of Mahābhairava.
Having first worshipped the moving seat (calāsana) and recited the mantra one hundred times according to the sequence,
the gurus should then perform the recitation upon the vardhanī vessel for one-tenth of that number.
Thereafter, one should worship the lords of the directions with their respective names, using [mantras for] invocation and weapons;
having placed the *vardhanī* vessel following the *ghaṭa*, one should then cause it to be circled.
Proclaiming the command of Śaṅkara from the beginning to the end of the eastern quarter,
he then released streams of water while conquering the interior of the root.

First, having indeed held the *kumbha* (vessel), and afterwards the *vardhanī* (augmented vessel) known as the weapon (*śastra*), having placed those two in their respective positions and bowed, one should then speak this: || 21 ||
O Śakra and other guardians of the quarters, accompanied by your vehicles and weapons,
protect my sacrifice with effort and vigilance by the command of Śiva.
One should worship Maheśvara Amṛtīśa together with his limbs (aṅgas) in the pitcher (*kumbha*) upon the complete seat, and Astra-Bhairava in the *vardhanī* vessel. (23)
One should perform the mudrā known as the yoniliṅga with the liṅgamudrā;
having placed the sword of Śiva upon the pitcher by the command of Śiva.
Having paid obeisance to Śiva residing in the *kalaśa* vessel, to the bow (*śārṅga*), to the *vardhanī* vessel, and to the weapons in their embodied forms, one should thereafter worship Gaṇa.
One should [worship] the white, four-armed deity with one face and three eyes,
seated upon a lotus partially shaded by Vāyu, in the petal of the northeast direction, as the Guru.
One should bathe the Lord of the World upon a pure, excellent, and beautiful auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha), which is golden and adorned with jewels.

Having performed the rites with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and so forth, as well as with pure water, and having interposed incense and flowers, one should worship the deity according to the prescribed rule preceded by mantras.
The wise one should bathe [the deity] as desired with even a hundred divine herbs, with sandalwood and agallochum water, or with cool water containing jewels. (29)
Then, one should install Śiva upon a golden throne adorned with the nine gems, covered with new, fine garments, and offered flowers and other articles.

Thus, having prepared the seat up to the limit of the purified enclosure, one should meditate upon the deity according to the prescribed rite and install him within the characteristic marks of the *liṅga*. || 31 ||
One should meditate upon the Lord of Gods within oneself, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons, resembling a pure pearl, and having the luster of crystal. (32)
The omnipresent Lord, resembling the lord of the Kunda flowers, cow's milk, and snow,
is adorned with ornaments such as white pearls and sapphire gems that are the very essence of perfection.
His limbs were smeared with white sandalwood paste, grey with powdered camphor;
he was vast with the nectar of the shimmering moon, immersed in many surging waves.
Seated in the center of a moon mandala, with one face and three eyes, he is seated upon a white lotus and stands in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana). || 35 ||
Four-armed and large-eyed, with hands granting boons and fearlessness, resembling the full moon, pure white, and filled with nectar. || 136 ||
One should visualize him holding a water-pot (kalaśa) that nourishes the world, and likewise, the full moon in his left hand. (137)
One should meditate upon him as being worshipped with entirely white offerings;
what need is there for much speaking here? He is the manifest ocean of nectar itself.
From that very source arises the nectar that sustains the entire universe;
one should then meditate upon it as resembling a wish-fulfilling gem, according to the distinctions of one's internal disposition. (39)
Having meditated thus, one should worship the deity with auspicious mental flowers within the heart-lotus for the sake of all spiritual attainments; thereafter, one should perform worship externally.
Offered with mental flowers by the practitioner, she is considered auspicious;
unwithered and supremely pure, she bestows liberation, grants accomplishment, and is auspicious.
Therefore, with every effort, one must certainly first perform the mental sacrifice; only afterwards should it be performed with elaborate material offerings.
Then one should invoke the deity conceived as having three bodies;
one should then place the limbs upon the petals according to the divisions starting from the southeast (āgneya).
With entirely white offerings, flowers, perfumes, and ointments;
with various and wonderful food offerings, and with excellent, well-burnt incense. || 44 ||
One should worship with various pleasing drinks according to the distinctions of one's disposition;
for the sake of pacification, one should worship Śiva with entirely white offerings.
During the rite of initiation, during consecration, during an earthquake, when a king is eminent, in the presence of thieves, famine, disease, and likewise in the peril of death; || 46 ||
In times of fear caused by spirits, ghosts, and demons, or from snakes and conflict, and for the sake of pacifying the flood of various obstacles, one should likewise employ many ritual requisites.
Then one should worship Amṛteśāna together with Mahāśrī;
one should meditate upon Bhairava as he gazes with a gracious look.
Having thoroughly mixed camphor, sandalwood, saffron,
and agallochum with "moon-water," one should smear the Lord Īśvara.
With *karṇikāra*, *vakula*, mango, and *viśoka* trees, with *campaka*, *karavīra*, and *kadamba*; with *kiṅkirāta*, fresh *mālatikā*, *kunda*, *pāṭali*, and intensely red lotuses; || 50 ||

With *kakana*, *dhūttūraka*, auspicious *puṇḍarīka*, *mallikā*, *ketakī*, *stagara*, blue lotuses, *pārijāta*, *arjuna*, blue water-lilies (*kahlāra*), *kuṭaja* flowers, as well as *sinduvāra* and *arka* flowers; || 51 ||
He who worships Maheśa— the sole embodiment of compassion— with various kinds of flowers, [offering] garlands hanging down to his throne;
And [he praised] the Goddess Mother Ajā, the Supreme Lord Lakṣmī, who removes the suffering of the three worlds and bestows fearlessness. || 52 ||
At the conclusion of the sound, one should steal the mantra while preceded by the ringing of a bell;
thereafter, [one should offer] agallochum mixed with guggulu and combined with clarified butter.
He should burn the finest incense before the Lord while meditating upon it—incense that generates clarity of mind and wards off all obstacles. (54)
One should offer as an oblation before Śambhu milk-rice, cakes, sweetmeats, sugar-candies, plantains, and maṇḍakas, having obtained them through gambling or by begging.
And also red śāli rice, accompanied by many side dishes.
One should offer as a gift curd and milk mixed with clarified butter.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer betel-leaf, a mirror, a lamp, along with an umbrella and chowries, all these together to Śambhu while reciting the root mantra. || 57 ||
It should be fumigated, consecrated with mantras, and entirely free from hair and other impurities;
it should then be washed and subsequently dried by the rays of the sun.
One should cover Śiva with these excellent cloths— produced in Cīna, Draviḍa, Saurāṣṭra, and Gauḍa— which are fine and smooth.
Having thus performed the worship with the five offerings according to the prescribed rule,
one should thereafter perform the recitation (japa) with a mind that is supremely focused.
Devoted to devotion, one should perform circumambulation, hymns of praise, and prostrations with the limbs touching the ground;
meanwhile, the preceptor, holding the *argha* vessel in one hand, should indeed proceed clockwise around the pure fire.

Then, the fire-chamber was provided with *kuśa* fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, clarified butter, parched grain, barley, fruits, grains, and white mustard seeds, along with various kinds of flowers; thereafter, the excellent preceptor arrived, carrying an offering in his hand. (52)
Whether it be square or circular, measuring one cubit or even more, the preceptor may act according to his own will; everything is accomplished through the realization of pervasiveness.
One should perform the pervasion of the sacrificial pit (kauṇḍilya) by means of the nature of Śakti;
having understood that [pervasion] as encompassing the pit, the Guru shall become the giver of all.
Until he, the knower of the six limbs, realizes the pervasiveness of both the sacrificial pit and the self, as well as that of the object to be accomplished, the bound soul, and the fetters.
As long as one plays like a child, how can there be accomplishment for him?
But he who knows himself to be of the very nature of Śiva and Śakti— (66)
Śiva is the bestower of all fruits, the most excellent, the creator, the omnipresent;
he is the fire consisting of the power of knowledge, pervading [all] through the distinction between the pervaded and the pervader.
The Guru is one who is born together [with the disciple], the creator of all, the giver of liberation, and the bestower of fruits;
he who, by means of honor, measure, and proof, finds the Self within his own breath is the Guru. (68)
Like an artisan, you are skillful and capable of producing various forms;
yet you do not grant liberation, nor do you bestow the fruit of spiritual perfection.
Therefore, the preeminent teacher should be possessed of knowledge and be a bestower of all things;
he should take refuge in Śiva, abide in Śiva, and be impelled by the power of Śiva.
He is free from the sense of "mine" regarding the entire world, for he abides in the form of Śiva;
endowed with will, knowledge, and action, he is an expert in the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva). || 71 ||
Whoever acts by the will of Śiva, established in the pervasion of knowledge—
for indeed, the power of mantra arising from the mouth of the Supreme Lord is inconceivable.

When there is conviction, liberation exists; otherwise, how could it come to be? (14)
But by the piercing of the Śāmbhava [nature], one is instantly freed from the objects of the senses;
and by that very freedom from sense-objects, one is liberated even while in this body. || 15 ||
How can one who has been pierced by that piercing, for whom the taste of pleasure no longer exists, become detached from sense objects once freed from [physical] pain? (16)

For even when the Śāmbhava [state] has been attained, one who is momentarily agitated by pride must, at that very moment, go to the presence of the Guru through the bliss of the Command (ājñānanda). 17.
Having understood the characteristics of the piercing rites (vedha) beginning with Bhūta and ending with Śāmbhava, the Guru should then bestow initiation upon a disciple who is a true devotee.
Then, with sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron, he should cause an auspicious mandala to be made in his own right hand, provided there with a lotus.

Having fumigated it with guggulu incense according to the prescribed procedure, the preceptor should place [the deity] within the mandala, filling it from the power of the moon (the first digit) up to its fullness.
The seat of the God of gods, Amṛteśa, is most beautiful;
upon it, one should invoke the Lord, together with his limbs [attendants] and his retinue.
Having indeed led [the practitioner] to the state of *unmanī*, even if one is unable to recite the principal mantra,
one should worship that stainless one who possesses the form of Mahābhairava.

Endowed with the three mandalas and radiant like a mass of lightning, [it should be worshipped] with incense, fine sandalwood, flowers, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, and excellent lamps. || 23 ||
Having worshipped Śiva, who is well-pleased, with various kinds of food offerings, and having meditated upon Śiva along with his limbs (attendants) upon the head of the child at that time; 24.
One should offer the short *śiva* syllable while meditating on the child who is the very self of Śiva;
then, according to the prescribed rite, one should worship Śiva in the hand of that same child.
Then, having imparted the supreme Mṛtyuñjaya mantra into the ear of the disciple according to the prescribed rite, the Guru [unified] the disciple with the essence of the mantra.

Having performed the fivefold worship for the sake of the Noble Ones, [the disciple] should then joyfully look upon the Guru, who is the Great Lord Maheśvara, the Lord of Immortality, while scattering flowers.
The naming of the disciple, preceded by the description of the falling of that flower, shall end with the words "Śivāmara. (28)
Having removed the cloth-band called the "eye," he should subsequently open [the eyes] with a golden probe placed at the base,
while reciting the Mūrti-mantra.
One should then recollect that the disciple’s eyes have become stainless;
thereafter, [one should worship] Śiva, the Lord of Amṛteśa together with his limbs (sāṅga), accompanied by Mahāśrī.
One should diligently offer the worship to the Child [the disciple] by means of the Śiva-kumbha, the Astra-mantra, and the Vardhanī;
thereafter, one should offer worship to the Fire and then lead him into the presence of the Deity.

Having paid homage to Maheśāna with devotion, the Guru, with a concentrated mind, should offer one hundred and eight sesame seeds into the fire while reciting the root mantra for the sake of the child.
It is for the removal of defects such as deficiency, for that which is firmly established in the hand of Śiva, and for the dispelling of ill omens; it is endowed with internal inclusion. (33)
Likewise, one should discern the student’s removal of sin from the characteristics of the fire here.

Regarding this, it is said: "If the fire, while consuming the oblation, trembles, bursts apart, has the smell of excrement, emits sparks, or touches the ground, one should know that there is a transgression by the child. (34)
A fire that is fragrant, pleasant to the touch, glossy, curling to the right, and radiant is auspicious; one should recognize this as a good omen for the child.

Having thus understood the characteristics of the fire, one should first offer one hundred and eight oblations of excellent sesame seeds with the Astra-mantra for the purification of the child's impurities.
Afterwards, the Guru should be honored with loads of gold, excellent seats, and wonderful ornaments inlaid with rubies and pearls. (37)
Having given sandals made of ivory and likewise of various jewels set with nine gems, as well as a golden throne, an umbrella, and two auspicious chowries; 38.
With jewels, pearls, and great lordly elephants; with camels, rams, cattle, and the like; and with excellent, auspicious territories such as fields, villages, and districts. (39)
Whatever causes satisfaction for the teacher when given together with [the disciple], all that should be given to the guru by the disciple in every way, without stinginess regarding wealth. (40)
Since everything from Kālāgni up to Śiva is dependent upon the Guru, when he is satisfied, the Lord himself—the very nectar—is satisfied. (41)
And Śiva, acting for the universal grace of all beings, appears in the form of the preceptor;
therefore, one should not employ a human-like intellect toward the spiritual teacher.
This is because of such scriptural statements.
Now, he who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva, and he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru;
the Supreme Lord is the savior of those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence. (43)
Then, together with his wife, his sons, and his servants, attendants, and vehicles, the disciple, with a joyful mind, should present himself before the Guru. (44)
"O my Guru, please accept this body and all else as your own, through my self, my mind, my speech, and especially through my actions, in the state of servitude. (45)
O Lord, for the sake of service, accept me who am wretched and afflicted;
having given the support of Your hand, lift me up, for I am unconscious. 46.
O Lord, you alone are the refuge for those who have committed great sins, as well as for those who fear worldly existence, just as water is for those afflicted by thirst. 47.
Having made a request to his own guru with hundreds of prostrations like a staff,
the disciple should offer his body, life-force, and wealth to the true gurus.
Thus has been described the initiation consisting of the knowledge of the nirvāṇa-piercing of supreme consciousness, characterized by all the principles, ending with the teacher’s fee.
Thereafter, the proclamation of the *samaya* (vow) is described. As follows:
"One should subsequently proclaim the *samaya* as it has been taught in the *Āgama*, for the disciple who is bowed down with devotion and has approached the Guru. (1)
One should cultivate firm devotion to Śiva, to the Guru, to the sacred fire, and to the Śiva-āgama; with single-minded intent, one must never neglect the daily ritual practice.
One should not look at the naked wife of another, nor should one ever speak contemptuously of the Lord of Causes (Śiva), nor should one compel an unwilling woman [to have intercourse]. || 3 ||
One should not desire to kill a living being, nor should one engage in disputes with others; one must not revile the country, nor should one treat an artisan with contempt.
One should never associate with those who are devoid of the conduct of the tradition, those who follow other scriptures, or those who are intent on reviling Śiva.
Gambling, false speech in the presence of the Guru, yawning, laughter, wearing a turban, and riding in vehicles or on mounts. (6)
The nurturing of children, gazing at the faces of women, adorning oneself with mirrors, and looking upon the excellence of the world—these are [the concerns of the ignorant]. (7)
The chewing of betel-leaf, the carrying of a small knife or weapon, covering the head with a cloth, and sitting in close proximity [to others]. || 8 ||
The binding of a staff, sitting with a meditation-band, and these other practices as well—the young practitioner should avoid them in every way. (9)
Whether standing far away or nearby, at every sight [of him],
the disciple should never fail to prostrate before his own guru with a staff-like salutation.
This [body] is as pure as a clod of earth or a stone on the ground; no deliberation should be made regarding this. One should prostrate upon seeing the Guru. (11)
Rising up with haste, the disciple, being humble and with palms joined in reverence, should follow behind the teacher as he walks, having seen him. (12)
O child, through constant beholding, touching, and likewise chanting the praises of the Guru, as well as through meditation upon him, the great sin of the disciple is destroyed by Śiva.
The deities, as well as the yakṣas, vidyādharas, and kimpuruṣas and others, bestow their grace upon a true disciple who is devoted to his guru.
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in the Guru; for the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, are dependent upon the Guru. 15.
Having thus heard the condensed ritual procedure and having prostrated before the guru with his whole being, the disciple should thereafter perform the worship of the day and night.
One should provide food, excellent garments, and likewise sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to ascetics and brahmins, as well as to actors and singers.
Having taken up a handful of flowers and performed three circumambulations, one should offer oneself to the Guru, the Supreme Lord. (18)
And those others who belong to the lineage of the guru’s succession and have been previously initiated—those gurus also should be known as highly venerable, just like one's own guru. (19)
Regarding those who are younger brothers, as well as others such as brothers' sons,
he observes their common fitness or lack thereof through the sequence of knowledge, ignorance, and so forth.
The pledge must be protected in every way, just as it is established in every scripture;
for all accomplishments have that as their root and are situated everywhere upon it.
By the violation of the *samayas*, one becomes a transgressor of the scriptures;
when the scriptures are transgressed, the Lord Maheśvara himself is abandoned. (22)
When the Supreme Lord is lost, the latent impressions (saṃskāras) and so forth are lost;
consequently, with those impressions lost, one is cooked in the hells and other such realms. || 23 ||
Therefore, one must not abandon the commitments (samaya), even at the cost of one's life;
for the accomplishments (siddhis) come to dwell with one who abides by the commitments.
Though enraged, he might cause mountains to fall, dry up the lords of the oceans, and shatter both rocks and trees; yet, by virtue of observing the rules of his vow, he remains restrained.
While bathing, worshipping a deity, being ill, with disheveled hair, or lying down, a disciple should not bow to the guru; he should instead pay homage with his body and mind.
However, when it is necessary, a disciple should not prostrate before the guru while he is anointed with oil, eating, engaged in sexual intercourse, shaving his head, or vomiting. (27)
One must not sit down first in the place where the head [of the teacher] is located, nor on a high seat in the presence of the guru,
nor in a secluded spot while the guru is situated beneath an image of Viṣṇu.
When he has arrived at the teacher’s residence, the disciple, having avoided elaborate adornment and remaining self-restrained, should first bow to the door and then enter.
Just as copper becomes gold through contact with an alchemical elixir, even so, through contact with a guru, the destruction of the disciple's sins occurs. (30)
A disciple should always serve near the feet of the guru; he should not speak much, but should speak only when told, "Speak. (31)
When commanded by the teacher, one should perform the task oneself and not have it done by another;
likewise, one should avoid washing his feet, sleeping, or stretching out one's legs [in his presence]. (32)
One should avoid cutting one's nails or hair in the presence of the guru;
or, having obtained permission, one may do so out of the guru's sight.
A woman who was previously desired by the guru during their association must not be desired even in thought by the disciple, just like his own mother. (34)
One should never engage in verbal debate with one's teacher due to an excess of learning, out of pride, or because of an increase in physical beauty or wealth. (35)
One should always worship the Guru’s consort, his seat, his sandals, his shoes, as well as his swing and his vehicle, just as one would worship the Guru himself. (36)
When the Guru has arrived at the abode for the sake of service and has gone somewhere outside,
the disciple should likewise worship the implements used by him.
One should always behave toward his wife, his sons, his brother, and his friends, as well as toward his circle of kinsmen, exactly as one would toward a guru.
When one bows to the deity or to one's own guru, or when the guru [bows], then one should bow oneself as well and demonstrate devotion toward the guru.

When something has been said by the Guru, one should speak only after first receiving his command; even when saying "Jī-u," one should do so [only thus]. The person of small intellect who does not protect the conduct of the *samaya* with devotion...
"He goes to a terrible hell"—such is the command of the Supreme Lord.
In the most terrible Kumbhīpāka, likewise in the Asipatravana,
in Avīci and Raurava, and in the blazing house of molten copper.
In this manner, as long as the world endures, one who has committed an offense against the Guru’s command is cooked in the hell that arises with its seven crores of divisions.
In the case of a staff, or likewise in battle, on a path infested with thieves, or when a life-threatening danger has befallen one's guru, one may here abandon even one's own life.
One who is well-marked with the auspicious signs of Śiva—whether by rudrākṣa beads or with sacred ash—should be honored with respect like a guru, even if he has arrived alone. 57.
One should not inquire of a guest who has come to one's house regarding his lineage or name; rather, having meditated undisturbed upon the hells, one should enjoy him with pleasure. (58)
Alternatively: All this—the three worlds with their moving and non-moving beings—is to be understood as equal, since it is seen manifested through the signs of Śiva and Śakti. (59)
Therefore, the wise practitioner of meditation should meditate upon everything as belonging to Maheśvara;
hence, one should worship the entire multitude of principles (tattvas) and take refuge in them.
Anger, intoxication, and pride should never be grasped;
having worshipped the external signs and the city, one should afterwards worship the internal.
For it is said: Just as an oblation offered into a fireless pit filled with ashes is in vain, so too is the worship of Śiva by one devoid of devotion. 62.
Thus ends the section on proclaiming the rules of conduct for the disciple.
The initiation into the twenty-six principles has already been explained in due order;
thereafter follows the initiation into the five kalās, which consists of nine principles.
Initiation consists of the three principles and bestows liberation;
likewise, initiation consisting of a single principle is auspicious, leading to liberation and absorption.
Having thus composed this work, which is endowed with ritual action and esteemed by the world,
it was narrated in prose style to a disciple possessed of devotion.
Thereafter, one should make it possessive of knowledge, as demonstrated by the sixfold piercing; this, described through the analysis of the lotus, bestows liberation while living. || 4 ||
This brilliant Netrodyota, which dispels the darkness of ignorance and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is supreme; let the teachers worship it. (5)
This is the commentary on the Netrodyota of the Lord Amṛtīśa,
which has arisen from the Kula and Akula and is well-illuminated by the initiation of knowledge.
Thus, having reflected upon this *Maheśadīkṣā* composed by me, along with its brief commentary, according to the prescribed rule within my own heart,
may the skillful and boon-bestowing teachers, having abandoned all impurity and reflected well within their hearts, accept it with discernment.
This clear commentary on the initiation of Bhairava Amṛtīśa, composed by Viśveśvara, may it bring wonder to virtuous people. (8)

Having cast aside stinginess and having reflected with reason, and having deliberated with the virtuous regarding initiation into Maheśa— which was composed by Viśveśvara— those excellent teachers should indeed practice it properly with fully awakened minds. 9.
This brief commentary on initiation has been composed by me with the exuberance of my own devotion;
Śarva does not know everything, therefore, O teachers, please forgive me. (10)

Nevertheless, Viśveśvara [bestowed] the *dīkṣākrama*— the great scripture of all Śaiva meanings— which contains within it the essence of all principles (*tattva*), belonging indeed to the Moon-crested God whose form is the Absolute (*tatvamūrti*).
This was composed by me, Jñānapramati. || 11 ||
The Lord of the Universe (Viśveśvara) has established the lineage of the *yojanātikula*, as well as the supreme state of Śiva, Gāruḍa, Vaināyakya, Cāṇḍamātaka,
and Saura; he has also established the authentic sequence of initiation (*dīkṣākrama*) according to the ritual of the venerable Candrāmṛtabhairava.
Born from the mouth of Śambhu, it was composed by him with the intent of the Veda.
[Thus ends the *Apratihata-mahādīkṣā-suṭippaṇaka*, extracted from the essence of the intention of the collection of scriptures of the seven streams of Śiva, which illuminates the *Amṛteśanetra*.]
